newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan wants major firms to slow China investment.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan wants major firms to slow China investment.

text.p: Frustrated by a political impasse with China and a sagging economy, Taiwan wants local firms, especially conglomerates, to put their money in Taiwan instead of China, officials said on Friday.
"It is time to slow our investment in the mainland," Chiang Ping-kun, Taiwan's top economic policy maker, told Reuters in a telephone interview.

"Relations between both sides of the Taiwan strait are at their low ebb. The mainland side has not shown any genuine and sincere response to our propsoal for talks," said Chiang, who heads the Council for Economic Planning and Development.
"At this moment, we should not put all our eggs in one basket."

China angrily suspended semi-official talks in mid-1995 after President Lee Teng-hui's private but high-profile visit to the United States, which Beijing said showed Taiwan wanted independence rather than reunification with the mainland.

Both sides have expressed willingness to resume talks in recent months, but Beijing has stopped short of letting them happen, saying Taiwan should show sincerity by dropping efforts to raise its international profile.

Taiwan and China have been rivals since a civil war divided them in 1949 and Beijing still regards the island as a renegade province. Though all investment in China must be government approved, Taiwan remains concerned that its economy may become too dependent on China -- and hence politically vulnerable.
President Lee said in August the island needed to review its policy of targeting China as its main market to avoid over-dependence on the mainland for investment.
In addition to the political row with China, officials said an increasing number of huge investments by local conglomerates in China were hurting the "Asian dragon" economy.
"Huge investments in the mainland by Taiwan companies do not help the local economy," Huang Ching-tang, deputy executive secretary of the Investment Commission, said by telephone.
"Local businesses, especially major-capital companies, should invest more in Taiwan at the time when the domestic economy is slugglish," Huang said.
In August, the island's statistics directorate revised its economic growth forecast for all of 1996 to 5.89 percent, well below the 6.17 percent it projected in May.
But officials denied the government was tightening its economic policy towards China.
"Our economic policy (towards China) remains unchanged. We just hope investors can take all (the) factors into account when considering investments in China," Chiang said.

Huang said his agency had received no instruction to tighten reviews of mainland-bound investment projects but added the government was using "moral persuasion" to convince big businesses to take the lead and slow their steps.

Taiwan's food giant President Enterprises announced on Thursday it had abandoned plans to build a US$100 million power plant in China, and said it would instead invest more than T$30 billion (US$1.1 billion) in local projects over two years.

On August 16, giant Formosa Plastics Group said it was ending a deal to build what would have been the biggest Taiwanese project in China to date, a US$3 billion power plant project in coastal Fujian province.
Some 30,000 Taiwanese companies have poured more than US$20 billion into China since a political thaw in the late 1980s.
But Eric Liu of National Securities said the cooling of investment interests in the mainland may be only temporary.
"In the long term, Taiwan firms' investment in China is an inevitable trend that cannot be stopped," Liu said.
